description.narrative: 1. In Punjab, the regulation on social security contributions by Domestic Workers has been formally notified, marking a significant step towards ensuring their comprehensive welfare. Under this regulation, DWs are required to make contributions to a designated social security fund. This contribution system enables DWs to access a range of social security benefits. The notified regulation not only recognizes the invaluable role of DWs in society but also demonstrates the government's commitment to uplift their socio-economic status and provide them with a safety net that fosters dignity, stability, and improved quality of life. 2. The Domestic Workers' (DWs) Act, facilitated by comprehensive technical support, has paved the way for the establishment of an essential endowment fund aimed at enhancing the well-being of domestic workers. The Act, driven by a commitment to improve the working conditions and rights of DWs, has harnessed expert guidance to create a sustainable financial resource using Govt of Punjab's resources. Through this endowment fund, DWs will gain access to crucial financial assistance, healthcare provisions, educational opportunities, and skill development programs. 3. Provincial Bureau of Statistics has institutionalised tools to measure decent work deficits on HBWs and DWs. This has enabled generation of meaningful information that the government of Punjab has committed to use to inform investments in the care economy 4. A Roadmap for Decent Work for Sanitation workers in Pakistan developed 5. . A disability network by employers organizations established in May 2022 6. Employers pledge to promote Decent Work for Domestic Workers notified 1-2. The ILO, with RBSA funding, mobilised technical assistance to develop concept notes and TORs for the social security scheme for DWs in Punjab The ILO, with RBSA funding, advocated and provided technical advisory support to promote the ratification of C189. C189 has been added to the national ratification plan of the Government of Pakistan. The ILO, with RBSA funding, was also used to facilitate strategic partnership building and strengthening to collaborate with parliamentarians to influence relevant legislation for social security coverage of domestic workers in all four provinces. 3. The ILO, with RBSA funding, developed data gathering tools for provincial statistics institutions to gather data on the informal economy including HBWs and DWs for the first time, this support is now mainstreamed 4-6. The ILO, With the assistance from Government of Japan, provided inputs to the Roadmap and promoted formal support by constituents in Pakistan to vulnerable groups including DWs, Sanitation workers, and persons with disabilities.

description.narrative: 1. Led by Ministry of Overseas Pakistanis and Human Resource Development and by Departments of Labour in the provinces of Sindh and Punjab, an integrated programme on FPRW in the garment sector has been launched. An institutional governance mechanism has been put in place at national and provincial levels. The programme has undertaken an integrated assessment of the level of compliance with FPRW at the sectoral level focusing on textiles in two provinces using ILO's Compliance Assessment Tool by addressing all dimensions of FPRW. No child labour or forced labour has been identified in participating enterprises, but the following was noted: failure by factories to meet the provincial quota on workers with disabilities, provisions on maternity, and childcare. 2. 2 agricultural employers associations were established in 2023 (Sindh, Punjab). The Labour and Human Resources Department, Government of Sindh has drafted Rules for Women Agricultural Workers Act 2019 through two tripartite consultations to provide recognition of women's work in agriculture and related sectors, promote and protect their rights, ensure their participation in decision-making, and foster their empowerment. Resource Mobilization Strategy for the EFP was developed which would help continued pursuit and advocacy with the Governments (Federal and provincial) and other relevant organizations to integrate FPRW in their programs and policies. A strategic framework for the Workers Employers Bilateral Council to promote FPRW in the cotton supply chain was developed. Improved respect for FPRW among 3,055 (2,284 women) within cotton-growing communities, with 1,976 women linked to social protection schemes and welfare programs. 10 Bipartite agreements signed between the Pakistan Workers Federation and Cotton Farmers to support cotton workers in cotton growing areas in South Punjab. 1. With support from the Governments of Australia and Pakistan and the European Union, the ILO provided technical assistance, including capacity building, regular interaction, drafting ToRs and documents, supporting evidence base, and analysis to the constituents which contributed to the achievement of the results. After a decade of lobbying, consultations and technical support, grounds were established to initiate the pilot project on Better Work in March 2022. The ILO, with funding support from the EU, DFAT and the Government of Pakistan, has developed a compliance assessment tool, which covers several areas of both international and provincial labour standards (labour is a devolved subject under Pakistan’s constitution and therefore the legislative frameworks are specific to Sindh and Punjab, where the BWP pilot is operating). The CAT covers child labour; forced labour; discrimination; freedom of association and collective bargaining; contracts and human resources; compensation; working time; and occupational safety and health. The ILO has undertaken assessments in 40 enterprises to date. 2. With the support of a public-private partnership with INDITEX, Industria del diseno textil S.A on FPRW in the cotton supply chain, the ILO facilitated the establishment/organization of 2 agricultural employers associations in the Sindh and Punjab Provinces. The ILO is supporting the review of the Rules for Sindh Women Agricultural Workers Act 2019 and the organization of two tripartite consultations on the subject matter. The ILO provided support for the development of a resource mobilization strategy for the EFP to promote the integration of FPRW within programmes and policies of governmental and other relevant organizations. The ILO also provided technical support for the development of a strategic framework for the Workers Employers Bilateral Council of Pakistan (WEBCOP) to promote FPRW in the cotton supply chain.

description.narrative: The Forward Gear Workers Union with CBA status, Colony Textile Mills Workers Union Multan with CBA status, and Millat Tractors Workers Union with CBA status have successfully negotiated and developed comprehensive Collective Bargaining Agreements (CBAs) in collaboration with their respective employers. These agreements are emblematic examples of proactive measures taken to address the specific gender-related requirements of the women workforce within these establishments. Central to these CBAs is establishing Gender-Based Violence (GBV) Harassment Committees, with a strong emphasis on ensuring adequate representation of women on these committees. Recognizing the unique needs of lactating women workers, the CBAs underscore the provision of suitable facilities such as lactation rooms, and transportation for women by implementing pick-up and drop-off services. and other essential benefits such as paid maternity leaves, reinforcing the understanding that a supportive workplace embraces and empowers women through critical life transitions. The ILO advocated and provided technical support through workers organisations and social dialogue collective bargaining agreements to promote gender inclusive provisions. The ILO also shared knowledge on how more inclusive CBAs are designed based on ILO's experience.

description.narrative: The capacities of the constituents were strengthened to be part of 30 District Vigilance Committees (DVCs), with 6 being notified during the reporting period and promoting Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work. Building on the promulgation of the Women Agriculture Workers Act for Sindh in the last biennium, the Government of Sindh developed Rules of Business to implement this legal instrument. They facilitate the operationalisation of the Act and empower enforcement agencies to ensure its application. Targeted due diligence mechanisms on Child Labour were developed with support of Employers' Federation and piloted in 12 ginning and spinning companies in Sindh and Punjab. A Module on Protecting Children and Communities’ Exposure to pesticides was adopted by the Punjab Provincial Agricultural Extension Services and included in the Farmer Field Schools training of trainers. 42 Decent Work Cotton Resources Centres were established to serve as education and information centres. Over 1,600 children were kept out of child labour through accelerated schooling and reintegrated into the school system. More than 200 youth and women received vocational training and gained access to income-earning opportunities within the cotton, textile, and garment value chains. Additionally, 42 community-based multi-stakeholder monitoring and remedial mechanisms were established to combat child and forced labour at village levels Two farmers' associations and two trade unions were established and strengthened within the lower tiers of supply chains. The Girls Guide Association is implementing a "Each One Teach One" program involving 1,844 patrols for children withdrawn from labour. 10 Bipartite agreements were signed between Pakistan’s Workers Federation and Cotton Farmers to support cotton workers in South Punjab. With the support of the European Union (EU), the ILO provided technical support for the organization of several meetings to reactivate DVCs through a robust action plan for addressing child labour in 30 districts in Sindh. The ILO provided technical assistance for the development of the Rules of Business for Women Agri Workers Act in Sindh, thereby mobilising women in agriculture and facilitating a dialogue on protection and effective rights to organise. With funding from the EU, the ILO partnered with the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) to mobilize tools and knowledge resources to enhance the capacities of extension workers. With the support of the ILO, community-based organisations were empowered to strengthen their efforts in mobilizing Decent Work Cotton Resources Centres and implementing community-based monitoring mechanisms to identify and report child labour instances.
